newsitem.title: GERMANY: German, French ministers see EMU start on time.
newsitem.headline: German, French ministers see EMU start on time.

text.p: The German and French junior European ministers said on Wednesday Europe's planned single currency would go ahead on time in 1999 and said they were working hard to keep bilateral relations close.

Franco-German ties have been strained since France's new Socialist government suggested it would not meet the three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) entry criterion to qualify for the planned 1999 launch of the euro.

They met after France's Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn was quoted as telling a parliamentary committee on Wednesday that a key audit due next week would show a deficit above 3.5 percent of GDP this year.
But the two ministers were adamant France remained committed to joining European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Some say the German-French motor is sputtering. We are both working to make sure that does not happen," Werner Hoyer, state secretary in the German Ministry, told journalists.
"We have discussed the challenges facing us. First is to start the third stage of economic and monetary union on time and under the criteria as laid out in the treaty," Hoyer said.

France's junior minister for European affairs Pierre Moscovici, sipping a glass of the local Koelsch beer at Hoyer's side, said both countries would make sure EMU went ahead on time and under the Maastricht entry criteria.
Asked how strong France's commitment was to joining EMU, Moscovici said: "Let's do it. The euro is coming -- at the planned time and under the conditions seen in the criteria."
Hoyer agreed with his French counterpart.

Moscovici, who was rebuked by French Prime Minister Lionel Jospin last month for suggesting France was not fully committed to the euro single currency, said he was sure the project would go ahead as planned.
"We have spent our time talking about the interpretation of the criteria. I can assure you that Germany and France are taking all the necessary steps to achieve them," he said.

Moscovici said Franco-German relations were an absolute priority and said the two ministers would aim to coordinate some of their visits abroad, particularly to the new candidates for European Union membership.

Jospin commissioned the audit soon after being elected on June 1, partly to help decide what measures are necessary for France to join a single European currency. The results are being watched closely to see how far the government is prepared to go to bring the deficit towards three percent of GDP.
Jospin's office in Paris said on Wednesday he would meet Kohl in late August.
